lessons.title: पानीयम् (pānīyam) — "water," the thing to be drunk
lessons.gloss: water — "the thing to be drunk," and the exact word your neighbors' पानी grew from

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page

segments.text: Say "Sanskrit is dear to me." (Saṁskṛtaṁ mama priyam.) Every word so far has named an action. Now for the nouns you would actually reach for — starting with the one you would ask for first.

utterances: Sanskrit: पानीयम्. sound: pānīyam. meaning: water.
Sanskrit: पिबति. sound: pibati. meaning: he, she, or it drinks.

segments.text: पानीयम् (pānīyam) is neuter, and its final -म् marks that — a whole family of everyday nouns ends this way, and it will keep coming back this chapter.
पा is pā, the long-ā you have said since नाम. नी stacks न na under the long-ī sign ी. यम् closes it: y, the inherent a, then म् with its vowel stripped by the halant — pā-nī-ya-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the thing to be drunk

segments.text: पानीयम् (pānīyam) is built on the root पा (pā), "to drink," plus -अनीय (-anīya), a suffix meaning "fit to be ed." Literally: the thing that is to be drunk.
The root is PIE peh3-, "to drink." Latin took it into potare, and from that English has potion and poison — a drink, and a drink gone wrong.

Eastward, पानीयम् (pānīyam) wore down through Prakrit pāṇīya into the everyday water-word of the daughter languages: Hindi पानी (pānī), Gujarati pāṇī, and, in the Bangladesh register of Bengali, pani — every one तद्भव, worn down by ordinary speech, not carried over whole. Sanskrit's own oldest water-words, जल and उदक, took a different road entirely; this is not that word.

segments.instruction: the root and its suffix — pā "drink" plus -anīya "fit to be"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the root and its suffix — *pā* "drink" plus *-anīya* "fit to be"]

segments.instruction: the worn-down grandchildren — pānī, pāṇī, pani

segments.text: What does पानीयम् (pānīyam) literally mean, and from which two pieces? ("The thing to be drunk" — pā "drink" plus -anīya "fit to be".) Name two English words from the same PIE root. (Potion, poison.) Is Hindi pānī तत्सम or तद्भव? (तद्भव.) And how did you say "dear to me" last chapter? (Priyam.)

lessons.title: क्षीरम् (kṣīram) — "milk," and the dessert it left behind
lessons.gloss: milk — an origin scholars still argue over, and the dessert word it left behind

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "water," and the root it is built on. (Pānīyam; पा, "to drink.") Not every drink-word in Sanskrit has so tidy an answer.

utterances: Sanskrit: क्षीरम्. sound: kṣīram. meaning: milk.
Sanskrit: क्षीर. sound: kṣīra. meaning: milk — the bare stem, still living inside Hindi khīr.

segments.text: Neuter again, marked by the same -म् as पानीयम् (pānīyam).
क्ष is a new stacked pair: क k fused under ष, the hissed retroflex s — together they say kṣa, one push, not two. Then the long-ī sign ी, र ra, and the neuter म् you already know: kṣī-ra-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — a disputed root, and a live dessert

segments.text: Where पानीयम् (pānīyam)'s history is settled, क्षीरम् (kṣīram)'s is not. One account traces it to an old Proto-Indo-European word for milk; another argues it was borrowed from a substrate language spoken where Indo-Iranian speakers first arrived in the region. Neither side has won.

What is clear is the family it sits in: Avestan xšuuidi- and Persian šir say roughly the same word, but as relatives, not children — all three come down from one shared Proto-Indo-Iranian ancestor, the way gṛhṇāti and English grab are cousins rather than the same word wearing different clothes.
The word's liveliest descendant is not a drink. Hindi खीर (khīr) is a sweet rice pudding cooked in milk — worn down, तद्भव — and English borrowed that dessert whole, as kheer.

segments.instruction: the dessert it became — khīr, borrowed into English as kheer

segments.text: Is क्षीरम्'s own origin settled or disputed? (Disputed — inherited, or borrowed from a substrate.) Are Persian šir and Sanskrit kṣīram parent and child, or relatives? (Relatives, from one shared ancestor.) What English word for a dessert comes from Hindi khīr? (Kheer.) And what does pānīyam literally mean? ("The thing to be drunk.")

lessons.title: अन्नम् (annam) — "food," the eaten thing
lessons.gloss: food, grain — literally "the eaten thing," built on the very root खादति left uneaten

needs: your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your eyes, so it is not fully a driving lesson. You will want your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the section called The letters in this word until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Say "milk" and "water." (Kṣīram, pānīyam.) One more thing you would ask for, and this one carries a root you already own.

utterances: Sanskrit: अन्नम्. sound: annam. meaning: food, grain.
Sanskrit: खाद्यम् अन्नम्. sound: khādyam annam. meaning: edible food — खादति's own adjective on it.

segments.text: Neuter, and -म् again — the third noun running.
अ opens bare, no consonant to carry it. न्न doubles न na onto itself, held a beat longer than one n would be. म् closes it, the same stripped-vowel neuter ending: an-na-m.

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — the eaten thing

segments.text: Chapter 7 taught खादति, the everyday word for eating, and set beside it its untaken cousin: अद्, PIE ed-, the very root of English eat, which Sanskrit keeps alive as अत्ति.

अन्नम् (annam) is built on that same अद्, plus the old participle suffix -न — "eaten." The d and the n fuse into the doubled न्न you just sounded out. Food, named this way, is not a thing but an event: the thing that has been eaten.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: three genders, one small system

segments.text: Every noun in this chapter has ended in -म्, and that is not coincidence: Sanskrit sorts every noun into one of three genders — masculine, feminine, and neuter — the same system that put a gendered form on the numerals back in Chapter 6, where the daughter languages inherited specifically the neuter forms, trīṇi and catvāri. This book teaches only the plain nominative singular of each noun, never the full run of cases and numbers behind it — but the gender is worth carrying, because it is not optional, and it is not guessable from meaning alone.

segments.text: What does annam literally mean, and which root is it built on? ("Eaten"; अद्, the cousin of English eat.) Which everyday verb shares that root without being it? (Khādati.) Which gender have all three nouns this chapter shared? (Neuter, marked by -म्.) And which gendered form did the numerals hand the daughter languages back in Chapter 6? (The neuter one — trīṇi, catvāri.) Name this chapter's three words. (Pānīyam, kṣīram, annam — the things you would ask for.)
